title.en: Describe alcoholic and lactic acid fermentation.

say.en: Idli batter rises overnight, milk turns to curd, and your legs ache after a long run. All three are about what cells do with pyruvic acid when oxygen is short. In this lesson: Describe alcoholic and lactic acid fermentation.
Name the enzymes involved.
Explain why fermentation releases little energy.

body.en: *Pyruvic acid*, the key product of glycolysis, has three major fates: lactic acid fermentation, alcoholic fermentation and aerobic respiration. Fermentation takes place under anaerobic conditions in many prokaryotes and unicellular eukaryotes. In alcoholic fermentation by yeast, pyruvic acid decarboxylase and alcohol dehydrogenase convert pyruvic acid to CO₂ and ethanol. Some organisms, such as lactic acid bacteria, and animal muscle cells during vigorous exercise when oxygen is inadequate, reduce pyruvic acid to lactic acid using lactate dehydrogenase. In both, NADH + H⁺ is reoxidised to NAD⁺, which lets glycolysis continue.

say.en: Pyruvic acid, the key product of glycolysis, has three major fates: lactic acid fermentation, alcoholic fermentation and aerobic respiration. Fermentation takes place under anaerobic conditions in many prokaryotes and unicellular eukaryotes. In alcoholic fermentation by yeast, pyruvic acid decarboxylase and alcohol dehydrogenase convert pyruvic acid to CO 2 and ethanol. Some organisms, such as lactic acid bacteria, and animal muscle cells during vigorous exercise when oxygen is inadequate, reduce pyruvic acid to lactic acid using lactate dehydrogenase. In both, NADH plus H⁺ is reoxidised to NAD⁺, which lets glycolysis continue. Yeast: pyruvate gives ethanol plus CO 2.

say.en: Pyruvic acid, the end product of glycolysis, has three possible fates, depending on the organism and on oxygen.
Without oxygen, muscles and lactic acid bacteria make lactic acid; yeast makes ethanol and CO₂. With oxygen, pyruvate is fully oxidised.
In both fermentations the NADH from glycolysis is oxidised back to NAD⁺, so glycolysis can keep running.
Fermentation releases less than seven per cent of the energy in glucose, and yeast poisons itself when alcohol reaches about 13 per cent.
Let us draw where pyruvic acid goes with and without oxygen.

caption.en: Without oxygen, yeast turns sugar into ethyl alcohol and CO2; some bacteria and our muscles make lactic acid instead. Only 2 ATP are gained per glucose, against up to 38 in aerobic respiration. Yeast poison themselves when alcohol reaches about 13%, so fermentation stops with sugar left over. Illustrative rates.
caption.kn: ಆಮ್ಲಜನಕವಿಲ್ಲದೆ ಯೀಸ್ಟ್ ಸಕ್ಕರೆಯನ್ನು ಈಥೈಲ್ ಆಲ್ಕೋಹಾಲ್ ಮತ್ತು CO2 ಆಗಿಸುತ್ತದೆ; ಕೆಲವು ಬ್ಯಾಕ್ಟೀರಿಯಾ ಮತ್ತು ಸ್ನಾಯುಗಳು ಲ್ಯಾಕ್ಟಿಕ್ ಆಮ್ಲ. ಗ್ಲೂಕೋಸ್‌ಗೆ 2 ATP ಮಾತ್ರ. ಆಲ್ಕೋಹಾಲ್ ಸುಮಾರು 13% ಆದಾಗ ಯೀಸ್ಟ್ ಸಾಯುತ್ತದೆ.

body.en: In both lactic acid and alcohol *fermentation* not much energy is released: less than 7% of the energy in glucose is released, and not all of it is trapped as ATP. The processes are also hazardous: the products are either acid or alcohol. Yeasts poison themselves to death when the alcohol concentration reaches about 13%. For complete oxidation of glucose to CO₂ and H₂O, organisms use the Krebs cycle (aerobic respiration), which needs O₂.

points.en: Less than 7% of glucose energy is released.
Net ATP in *fermentation* = 2 per glucose (from glycolysis).

steps.en: Fermentation products are hazardous; ethanol builds up in the medium.
